A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same work on subagging regularized M-estimators. Their text, equations, figures, tables, and complete appendices support comparison, including matching material across the appendix reorganization.

before.justification: V1 reports original simulations comparing empirical and theoretical risks, including 50-simulation averages and standard errors for Huber ensembles in Figure 2 and lasso ensembles in Figure 9.

after.justification: V3 retains the original simulations and adds finite-sample validation under anisotropic designs in Figure 8 and non-Gaussian covariate experiments in Appendix F.2.

M1.justification: Section 6.1 extends the specified component objective from coordinatewise penalties to a potentially nonseparable convex penalty Reg(b), through Equation (25). The subsampling, fitting, averaging, and observable EST risk-estimation procedures are retained.

E1.justification: Synthetic regression coverage expands beyond isotropic Gaussian features and random signals. Figures 8–11 add AR(1) correlated designs with deterministic signals, while Appendix F.2 adds Student-t20, Rademacher, and uniform covariates.

E2.justification: The matched comparisons retain their ridge/ridgeless, lasso/lassoless, and Huber-based comparators and ensemble variants. The appendix's replacement of 'Huberless' with LAD identifies the same zero-threshold limit, rather than introducing a new comparator.

E3.justification: Figure 8 introduces a validation protocol for error norms, trace quantities, and overlapping-estimator correlations, with n=1000, p=200, Huber threshold and penalty both 1, and t4 noise. The new non-Gaussian lasso experiment uses lambda=0.1; the retained Gaussian experiment still uses lambda=0.001. These are added settings, not demonstrated reruns of existing experiments.

E4.justification: Appendix F.2 adds robustness checks of Gaussian-derived predictions under three non-Gaussian covariate distributions. Figure 9 adds sensitivity analysis over AR(1) correlation strengths, and Figures 10–11 examine whether optimal subsampling and regularization findings persist with correlated features and deterministic signals.

E5.justification: The new Figure 8 reports standard deviations across 1000 simulation runs. Existing empirical-risk figures retain 50-run averages with standard errors, also used in Figure 15. The PDFs do not establish an increase in repetitions for the retained experiments.

E6.justification: New results show agreement between finite-sample statistics and anisotropic predictions in Figure 8, decreasing optimal subsample sizes and risks with increasing AR(1) correlation in Figure 9, and joint-tuning advantages in Figure 11. Figure 15 adds empirical agreement under non-Gaussian covariates. These extend the findings to new conditions; the matched earlier risk plots retain their principal results.

T1.justification: V3 adds Theorem 3 on joint empirical convergence for pseudo-Lipschitz functions and its Appendix B.3 proof. Theorem 1 extends uniqueness to both subsample ratios equaling one; Proposition 8 includes infinite ensembles while changing the optimization domain from (0,1] to (0,1). Section 6.1 and Appendix E add generalized Moreau analysis, Systems 5–6, Theorem 9, and an explicitly heuristic treatment of Conjecture 10.

C1.justification: The original abstract's central risk-characterization and regularization claims remain. However, the introduction adds a substantial contribution concerning anisotropic covariance, deterministic signals, and potentially nonseparable penalties, supported by a contraction theorem and an empirically investigated conjecture. V1 largely leaves these extensions as future work.

C2.justification: Section 5.2 adds an explanation of optimal small subsamples through reduced estimator correlation and avoidance of interpolation peaks. Section 3.4 newly qualifies recovery of oracle tuning parameters. Section 6.1 and Appendix E.2 distinguish established contraction results from conjectural risk limits and identify missing trace-concentration and Gaussian-independence arguments.

D1.justification: New figures document covariance structures, deterministic signal construction, sample dimensions, and tuning settings. However, v3 removes v1's Section 1.1 footnote linking the simulation repository and sklearn-ensemble-cv package, together with the package reference. The original data-generation recipes and computing acknowledgment remain.

R1.justification: Section 5 adds positioning relative to optimization-induced implicit bias, with citations including Gunasekar and colleagues and Chizat and Bach. Additional references support proximal analysis, tuning, and anisotropic results. The main related-work survey remains largely intact; several other reference changes merely update publication information.

P1.justification: Most existing prose and the main section sequence are retained. Local revisions clarify terminology and optimization, integrate footnotes into the text, move the correlation-sign discussion into Appendix A, and regroup supplementary experiments. These editorial changes accompany, but are distinct from, the substantial scientific additions.

P2.justification: V3 adds four anisotropic-design figures and the six-panel non-Gaussian comparison in Figure 15. Existing figures are resized or relocated, and captions provide clearer optimization-marker explanations. Figure 4's legend is corrected, and appendix captions replace misleading k/n descriptions with the plotted p/k quantity.

improvement.justification: V3 substantially strengthens theoretical coverage through the joint-distribution theorem and the full-sample uniqueness argument, while new simulations investigate important assumptions left untested in v1. The anisotropic extension also supplies concrete equations and clearly identifies the remaining proof obstacle. These gains outweigh the removal of code-access pointers, although that removal weakens reproducibility and the general anisotropic risk limit remains conjectural.
